name: Freya Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Freya, 27, and I'm a marketing coordinator at Fernway, an outdoor clothing brand that sells rain jackets and hiking gear, mostly online. I share a flat with my friend Jo, who teaches primary school. I've been there just over a year, and before that I worked in a café while applying for anything with 'marketing' in the title.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most of my day is the email programme: I plan the weekly newsletter, write the copy, pick the photos and set up the sends. I also write the little stories about customers who've climbed things in our jackets, which is my favourite bit. I use an AI tool now and then for subject lines when I'm stuck, but my manager Dev still rewrites half my drafts. What wears me out is the data side, the open rates and click reports, because I'm honestly not good with spreadsheets yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not that surprised, the subject-line tool was handy but never magic. At work I'd joke that Dev can keep rewriting my drafts the old-fashioned way. Online I probably wouldn't post anything, I'm more of a lurker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be nervous, because I'm the weakest on the team at data and the routine reporting is exactly what the tools do. Fernway also had a bad summer, sales were down about ten percent because it barely rained. So even with no AI shock, I'm not sure my role is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take an evening course in data and spreadsheets, the cheap online one Dev mentioned, starting in January. I'd keep my two months of savings where they are and try to add a bit. And I'd ask to own the customer stories officially, since that's the part I'm actually good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay, with a background hum. The world's the same, but my company had a soft year and I'm the newest in the team. I don't lose sleep, but I check the company Slack more than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned sales were down because it barely rained. How does that touch you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When sales dip, the first thing they cut is freelance budget and the second thing is the newest hire. I'm the newest hire. Dev told me not to worry, but he also said 'for now,' which I keep replaying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jo about it over dinner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Jo that a dry summer is a scarier threat to my job than any robot. She'd laugh, because teachers worry about completely different things. Then she'd make me write a budget, which I'd avoid for a week.

say: I'd say the **subject-line tool** was handy but never magic.
I'd joke that Dev can keep **rewriting my drafts** the old way.
think: She's the **weakest at data**, and routine reporting is what tools do.
A **dry summer** cut Fernway's sales by about ten percent.
do: Take a cheap **online data course** starting in January.
Ask to own the **customer stories** officially, her strongest work.
feel: Mostly **okay**, with a background hum of worry.
Checks company Slack more than she'd like as the **newest hire**.
S0.quote: A dry summer is a scarier threat to my job than any robot.
fieldNote: Her worry comes from a **weak sales year**, not from AI.
She knows the newest hire goes first and replays her manager's **'for now'**.
She already sees **customer stories** as the part of the job worth protecting.

steps.text: Enrol in a cheap online spreadsheet and data course in January
Ask her manager Dev to make the customer stories her official job
Add a little each month to her two months of savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules on this, like companies having to retrain people before cutting them. At work I'd say it more softly, something like 'let's make sure juniors get trained on the new stuff.' I might sign a petition or two online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job turns into checking what a tool writes, and there won't be three of us doing that. The newsletter, the subject lines, the reports, all of that is writing and checking, which is first in line. I'd probably keep a job for a while, but with fewer hours or a smaller title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools properly, every day, not just when I'm stuck, so I'm the one who knows how they work. I'd push to own the customer stories and the photo shoots, since those need a person talking to a person. And I'd try to get to four months of savings by cutting the weekend trips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a slow leak. Not a crash, but something's quietly going down and I can't find the hole. I'm a bit annoyed at myself for waiting for proof before learning things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get to four months of savings. What would you cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weekend hiking trips, which is ironic for someone at an outdoor brand. They're about 150 a month with train fares and food. I'd keep one a month and drop the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the team would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam, who does our product pages, because that's the most routine writing we have. Sam's lovely but hates change even more than I do. I'd probably try to drag Sam along to the training with me.

say: I'd say companies should **retrain people** before cutting them.
At work I'd ask softly that **juniors get trained** on the new tools.
think: Her job becomes **checking tool output**, and fewer people will do it.
She'd likely keep work but with **fewer hours** or a smaller title.
do: Use the **AI tools daily**, so she knows how they work.

Reach **four months** of savings by dropping weekend trips.

**Annoyed** at herself for waiting for proof before learning.
S1.quote: My job turns into checking what a tool writes, and there won't be three of us doing that.
fieldNote: Steady by nature, she'd move once the **change is proven**.
She protects the **human parts** of her job, like customer stories.
She worries for a **colleague** who hates change more than she does.

steps.text: Use the AI writing tool every day for newsletter drafts
Pitch to run the customer stories and photo shoots
Drop three weekend hiking trips a month to save 150
Sign petitions for rules on retraining before layoffs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we needed rules years ago. I'd be angry online, and I'd probably go to a march for the first time in my life. At work I'd ask HR straight out what the plan is for staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job just goes, probably in 2028 or the year after. Everything I do is screen work: writing, planning, reporting. The only thing that might last is going to events in person, and that's maybe five days a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent or food, and push the savings as far as they go. I'd look at jobs that are hands-on, maybe in Fernway's flagship shop fitting boots, because robots come three years later. My dad runs a small bike repair shop, so I might ask him if I could learn the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. Two years feels like nothing; it took me two years just to get this marketing job. There's a bit of me that feels stupid for picking marketing at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The bike shop with your dad. Is that a real option, or a comfort?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's real, but it's small. Dad makes enough for himself and not much more. I could learn to true wheels and fit gears, and that's hands-on, so I'd get the extra three years. After that, who knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jo when you got home the day this was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Jo we might need to find a cheaper flat by summer. She'd probably say teachers are safe, and I'd say only until 2031. Then we'd open a bottle of wine and look at rents in the next town.

say: I'd say this is why we needed **rules years ago**.
I'd ask HR straight out for a **staff plan**, and maybe march.
think: Her job goes in **2028** or soon after, because it's all screen work.
Only **in-person events**, about five days a year, might last.
do: Cut spending to **rent and food** to stretch her savings.
Apply to fit boots in Fernway's **flagship shop**, buying three more years.
Ask her dad to teach her **bike repair**.
feel: **Scared**, because getting this job alone took two years.
Feels **stupid** for picking marketing at all.
S2.quote: Two years feels like nothing; it took me two years just to get this marketing job.
fieldNote: She sees **hands-on retail and repair** as a three-year refuge.
Her **dad's bike shop** is a real but small fallback.
First march of her life shows how a **steady person** shifts under shock.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent and food only for the first months
Apply for a shop-floor job fitting boots at Fernway's flagship store
Learn wheel truing and gear fitting at her dad's bike shop
Look for a cheaper flat with Jo in the next town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's get governments to plan retraining now. I'd share things about it, and I'd join the union for my sector if there's one. At work I'd ask for a training budget for juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have about three years before my role really shrinks, because the tools would get better on the way. I'm not quick at new things, but I'm good once something is proven. Five years is enough for me to watch what works for other people and copy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first year learning the tools properly and asking what new jobs appear around them. Then, by year two, I'd decide between staying in marketing as the person who runs the tools, or training in something hands-on. I'd keep building savings, aiming for six months by 2029.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but with a plan forming. I like that I could watch others go first. It's still a ticking clock though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch others go first. Who would you watch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kezia, a friend from uni, uses AI for everything already. If my friend Kezia, who works at an agency, is still employed in 2029, I'll copy whatever she's doing. If she's not, I'll know to get out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your plan if your company cuts you in year two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have about four months of savings and Jo to share rent with. I'd probably take shop work while I figure it out. It wouldn't be the end of the world, but it would be the end of the plan.

say: I'd say we have five years for governments to **plan retraining**.
I'd join a **sector union** and ask for a junior training budget.
think: Her role shrinks in about **three years** as tools improve.
She'll **watch what works** for others and copy it.
do: Learn the tools properly in the **first year**.
Decide by year two between **running the tools** and hands-on training.
S3.quote: If my friend Kezia, who works at an agency, is still employed in 2029, I'll copy whatever she's doing.
fieldNote: She uses a friend at an agency as her **early warning**.
Five years suits her **steady** wait-for-proof style.
Being cut in year two would **break the plan**, and she knows it.

steps.text: Take a proper course in the AI marketing tools in the first year
Join the marketing and creative workers' union
Build savings to six months of expenses by 2029
Watch her friend Kezia's agency to decide by year two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if we use it, so let's use it. I'd talk about it at work as a training question, not a doom question. Online I'd share good examples of companies retraining people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine for maybe six or seven years, then I'd need to be somewhere else. I'd be 37 in 2036, which is young enough to start again. The part that worries me is that I'm not great at the job now, so I'm not sure I'd get the good roles in the meantime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get much better at the data side over the next two years, so I'm useful for longer. Around year four, I'd start training in something people-facing, maybe outdoor instruction, since I love hiking anyway. I'd keep saving and probably delay buying a flat until I know where I'm working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about the big picture, a bit unsure about myself. Ten years feels like a career's worth of time. It's me I'm not sure about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Outdoor instruction is quite a jump. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's hands-on, it's outside, and you need a person to keep a group safe on a hill. Robots might come in 2039, but I can't picture one leading a school trip up a mountain. And it's what I do every weekend anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd delay buying a flat. Is that a big sacrifice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, because my parents keep asking when I'll buy. But I'd rather rent for longer than buy somewhere and then have to move for work. Jo and I would probably just keep the flat we have.

I'd frame it at work as a **training question**, not doom.

steps.text: Take a data and reporting course over the next two years
Train for an outdoor instructor qualification around year four
Keep renting with Jo instead of buying a flat

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years is how long it took me to get this job, so starting again in two years feels impossible. What would help is paid training with a real job at the end, not just a certificate.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about how much luck is in this. If it rains next summer, the outdoor clothing brand I work for does well and I feel safe, whatever AI is doing.

headlineQuote: If it rains next summer, the outdoor clothing brand I work for does well and I feel safe, whatever AI is doing.
portrait: Freya is a **27-year-old coordinator** at an outdoor clothing brand, sharing a flat with Jo, a teacher.

In fast AGI she'd fall back on **retail** or her **dad's bike shop**.
With ten years she'd retrain toward **outdoor instruction**, her weekend love.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years isn't enough to start again.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** that leads to a real job, not just a certificate.
